messages.author: 4d367efe02bee69e
messages.subject: a conference paper using Stan
parts:
Hi,

I would like to report a conference paper using Stan, available at

https://forecasters.org/wp-content/uploads/gravity_forms/7-621289a708af3e7af65a7cd487aee6eb/2016/07/Smyl_Slawek_ISF2016.pdf


S Smyl, K Kuber - "Data Preprocessing and Augmentation for Multiple Short Time Series Forecasting with Recurrent Neural Networks",

36th International Symposium on Forecasting, Santander, June 2016


A very short summary: a generalized Exponential Smoothing algorithm fitted with Stan still beats quite advanced recurrent neural network-based forecasting system :-)

 


Big thanks to all Stan's contributors!


Regards,

Slawek Smyl

messages.author: cffcce570e30f29d
messages.subject: Re: a conference paper using Stan
parts:
This is very interesting. Thanks for sharing. I have worked with forecasting time series data (individual stock prices and of the mutual funds) in the financial sector. In the some of the models I have built with ANN, I have used leading indicators as well as opposite trending stock prices to improve upon the model fits and forecasting accuracy of the ANNs: for example, when examining the stock prices across multiple sectors during the 2008-2009 market downturn, I have used the prices of precious metals (Gold, Silver weighted combination) as well as bond market prices to use as control variables. I found that this helped the models. Did you use such variables in your models?
My modelling was fairly basic in that, I used multi-layer perceptrons for training and forecasting. For leading market indicators, I used the excellent data source from http://recessionalert.com/ (I'm only a subscriber, I still use their information to develop forecasts for my own portfolio)

Krishna

messages.author: 4d367efe02bee69e
messages.subject: Re: a conference paper using Stan
parts:
Hi Krishna,
The M3 data set is just a few thousands of univariate time series, without any regressor variables. Adding such variables to my "Stan model" could be easy in some cases and difficult in others, depending on how complicated is the influence of variables on the model. In the latter case I would gravitate towards using neural networks or tree-based algorithms.
The leading indicators for stock market - sounds good, but do they really exist? :-)

Regards,
Slawek

I should have added a caveat, "leading indicators when there is no panic selling or black swan events". In all seriousness though, the work done by Recession Alert is definitely worth looking into. The main papers thoroughly document how they derive the models with proper validation. If I can find the papers or the links to them I will post them back here.

Krishna
